utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We await -- is there a matter you wish to raise, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask that Ms. Marie O'Leary put forth our proposal on our behalf on the admission of evidence from the Milutinovic case. It concerns a filing of Friday, and we corresponded with the OTP. She would like to familiarise you with the outcome of that effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just to clarify, there was no filing on Friday; there was a discussion with the Prosecution about perhaps tendering the underlying documents to the -- of the Milutinovic transcript that were not tendered. They were ones that had been tendered by the Defence teams largely in the Milutinovic case. We had an e-mail today from the Prosecution that there was no objection to tendering these exhibits, so we were wondering if now would be a good time to list through those and receive numbers if so admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many are there?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: We have 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Eleven. And they were all tendered and received in evidence in the course of the Milutinovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I am sorry, Your Honour. I don't believe so. Two of them were discussed but were not tendered or admitted into evidence in Milutinovic; the remainder of them were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well the associated exhibits in Milutinovic come into one category. We will have to learn from you about the other two. Could you tell us about those two, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the other two were a transcript of testimony of Roland Keith in the Milosevic case, it was discussed, by, I believe, one of the Defence teams, it was not admitted into evidence. It was not tendered, I don't believe. Additionally, there was the ICTY statement of John Clark which was given a number of 6D106; it was also not admitted, but it was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis do we receive those?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that as they were discussed, it would give some context to the totality of the transcript. And as the Prosecution was not objecting, we thought that it might help round out the fullness of the transcript. Of course, if you would like, of course, Mr. Djurdjic can discuss it with the witness to give it a frame of reference in this case, if you would like, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Take, for example, the statement of a person, of Mr. Clark, what are we going to do with that statement if it is received in evidence? Do we treat it as evidence? And we have not seen the person, we don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. But I think that it will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it not the case that in the course of its, you say, discussion in the Milutinovic case, that any material portions of that statement would have been put to the witness and discussed by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're getting a wise nod.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: As I'm being directed over here, we would withdraw that application then as far as those do not clutter the record, if you would see it at fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the transcript in Milutinovic might help us enough with those.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you then tender the ten or eight is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nine --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- well, I'm nearly there, aren't I? And the list is with the court officer, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And there's no objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. They will then be received as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would you like us to read through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you have the list with the Court officer, he can probably do that and apply the number as you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll save time by a memo to follow setting them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. O'Leary. Are we ready now for the witness? Let's have the witness, please. Ms. Gopalan, you have something?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have some documents that we wanted to tender into evidence in a similar fashion to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were these tendered as exhibits in the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how many are there?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the Milosevic trial. And how many were there?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And they were referred to in the Milutinovic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And those that have not been admitted into evidence, five, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Five. There's no objection, I take it, to those?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no objections. We put that forth in any case. I believe this should be treated as it was with the Defence. If this concerns some exhibits from the Milutinovic and Milosevic case, then the transcript should suffice, and I believe some of these were not admitted as exhibits in the Milutinovic case. I believe that was your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with numbers in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would say that these are associated exhibits to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think they've been received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now we'll try for the witness once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. The affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And Mr. Djurdjic is continuing with his questions. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ciaglinski. I went through the Friday transcript. Could you please give precise and brief answers to my questions so as to be able to save time in that regard, although I wasn't limited per se during my cross-examination by the Chamber as opposed to the previous two cases you testified in, in any case, I'd like to have brief answers to keep matters as efficient as possible. Mr. Ciaglinski, on Friday, we were discussing your position and function you had with the Verification Mission. According to the information I found in some written and other statements, your position was at the headquarters of General DZ. You were coordinator or liaison officer with the VJ, the liaison officer was Mr. Guy Sands, and the coordinator for the KLA were for a while David Wilson; and once he took up another position, it was done by David Meyer. Is the information I gathered from the documents correct? Do you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that General DZ believed that the three of you were too many to submit reports to him, therefore he appointed his assistant from military matters to be your superior, Mr. Sinclair, to whom you reported and he reported to DZ in turn. And then after Sinclair, several people went through that post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely, no. When -- Sinclair was there for a very, very short time, and when he left, I wasn't aware that anyone really replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: According to the information I had on General DZ, it was David Meyer, then Piers Noble, and then Mr. Lovelock, if I'm pronouncing that correctly and if I took that down correctly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I understand now what you are saying and who you are referring to. Yes, Ben Lovelock was the last one, and this was a function -- a person that carried out this function, whether it was Sinclair or Ben Lovelock or Noble, it was to look after DZ 's office, it was like his personal assistant. And so he controlled the access to DZ. He would do office work for DZ. That was the main function of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Richard Heaslip, what was his position or function?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, like all of us, he had different functions at different times of the mission, as I did, so at one time he came into the headquarters for a brief time to take over as head of liaison, but he was then sent to Macedonia to run the evacuation. So he had different functions. And also Heaslip was also the regional commander of the region centred on Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the information on DZ, I've found that Richard Heaslip was the main liaison officer appointed by DZ in order to coordinate the three coordinators; do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a few weeks, for a very short period towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to go back to the head of mission, it was Ambassador Walker; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General DZ was deputy head of mission for operations, and Mr. Giovanni Kesler was deputy head of mission for the police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday you said, I don't know whether I'll put this correctly, but I believe you said that the major part of the Verification Mission or the level that concerned the bulk of cooperation with the Yugoslavian institutions was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that. What I think I said was that the highest level of cooperation, the highest level of the Cooperation mission was sitting in Belgrade, but the every-day running of the organisation and the problem solving was done in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you arrive at that conclusion, that the top level of the verification commission of the OSCE was in Belgrade, whereas in fact there were only seven personnel there? Maybe they had the closest ties with the mission in Belgrade, but concerning the meetings of Mr. Walker and Sainovic as well as Loncar, that must have taken place at a higher level than the level of Ms. Phelan who was in Belgrade at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree, nonetheless, that the Kosovo Verification Mission, or rather its head, was Mr. Walker and that you were all answerable to him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Walker was the only person authorised, based on the reports of the regional centres and his teams, to make decisions on the violations of the agreement and to undertake measures that he deemed appropriate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The final decision was always his, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Save for one occasion when you were also present when he was replaced by his deputies, and it was up to them to decide whether to issue a communique or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which occasion are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I mean the report that was sent concerning the incident at Dulje, and the kidnapping in Stari Trg? In any case, if you don't recall that, I will put some documents to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it exactly, but I am sure I can be reminded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I certainly will. There is a number of them. I'd like to go back to your arrival. When the Cooperation was discharged by a person by the name of Donna Phelan within the hierarchy of the mission, in your statement you talk about the method planned by Ms. Donna Phelan, it was called the method of maximum confrontation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Maximum assistance. Maximum resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to the Serbs. What did the method consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm not aware of it being called the system of maximum resistance, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I will read it out. In the English page 3, paragraph 2: "The method we used that had been originally planned by Donna Phelan was to resist to the maximum."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the word I used was confrontational.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. It should be the same confrontation in Serbian, I thought it was the same. I'm sorry I failed to mention the exhibit number. It's the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Djurdjic please repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was admitted in our case as P832, the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, what was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you explain Ms. Phelan's method? The method of confrontation, as you called it. What did that entail?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the result of not getting any response back to our -- to Ambassador Walker's letter about our methodology of carrying out the inspections. And so -- and also when we requested permission to inspect the barracks at the Commission of Cooperation, we were told we were not -- we would not be able to do that. So the only way to try and carry out the inspection was to actually turn up at the barracks at the main gates and confront the problem. And, you know, try and get in, try and discuss with the commander, even obstruct the gates if necessary, and to spend as much time as possible at the barracks observing what was going on just outside the barracks, which wasn't appreciated by the VJ; and so, therefore, you can only describe this as a confrontational technique. It's the only option we had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I understood, her method failed, whereas the method you introduced succeeded; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possibly because of my diplomatic training that I decided that maybe by talking and agreeing and discussing methodologies we might make more progress, and that's what we tried to do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned your diplomatic training, I believe that you said that you now work for the foreign office; did I gather that correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am employed occasionally on a as-required basis by the foreign office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a special department that you work for, or do you work for the various sections of it according to the needs at that moment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mainly work for two departments within the foreign office; one is the department for international development, and the other one is for the department that deals with conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It means if we see you in the field, there must be a conflict. Thank you. Ms. Phelan eventually left the Verification Mission; she took up a position for centre for intelligence gathering; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that she returned to the state department. She was a state department employee, so the American Foreign Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I know that. In any case, I wanted to learn from you, if you know, what it was that the centre actually did, what is the centre for information gathering or compiling?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea how the American system works or what departments it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, this centre for information gathering or compiling concerns the Kosovo Verification Mission. Yes, you said she went to the state department, although my information is different from that. But have you ever heard of the Blue Book or the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, I thought you were referring to the period after she left the mission completely. I didn't realise you were still talking about her moving to what we referred to as the fusion cell, which was the information gathering, collation, and interpretation department of which she headed up for a certain length of time, which created the Blue Book, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To the extent that you can recall, could you tell us something about the fusion cell, how it worked, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I worked on it for a time, so I probably know a little bit about it. Basically, the information that was sent and all the reports that were sent in from regional centres were collated, brought into the same location; people examined them; they then sort of looked at previous reports dealing with the same topics, and tried to create a picture. So we -- but it wasn't just incidents, it was the whole business of information gathering in Kosovo. So we gathered information about the VJ, what they were doing, where they were; the MUP, what they were doing, what type of units they were; designations on their uniforms if we saw any markings on the uniforms. And then we tried to forecast what might happen in the future, possible of variants of what the outcomes might be of various actions that had taken place. So that's the type of work the fusion cell did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, now I see why you were included as well, because I learned that the cell employed an analyst from the UK, Germany, and the US; and in the jargon it was called the KVM Intelligence Service?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the jargon it was known as the KVM Fusion Cell, because it fused the information together. But, you know, what is information gathering? Some people call it intelligence, some people call it whatever, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ciaglinski, you told us that you had three documents that were your Bible and you carried them always with you. If I'm not mistaken. One was the Geremek-Jovanovic Agreement, the second document was the Byrnes-Djordjevic Agreement, and the third was the 1199 Resolution. Am I correct? Are these the three documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the Shaun Byrnes, it was the Djordjevic -- sorry the Djordjevic-Byrnes; it was the Naumann-Clark, not the 1199. So the two you mentioned, but not the 1199. The third one was the Klaus-Naumann document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Clark-Naumann, you're right. Let me go back to that. Weren't these three agreements the basis for the UN Resolution 1199?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly two of them were, I don't think -- the Byrnes-Djordjevic was outside that because the -- I think the Resolution 1203 which followed 1199 confirmed the workings of the mission under -- using those two agreements, including those two agreements in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it was a long time ago, that's why I'd like to show you the 65 ter document P456. We'll refresh our memories. That's the 1199 UN resolution from September 1998, and you will see that it preceded these three documents, one of which I had gotten wrong. I'd like us to discuss briefly -- there, there it is. It's the 23rd September, 1998. This is the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see page 2 in English, please. I'd like to tell the legal officer, we don't need on the screen the B/C/S version. We need only the English version for the witness and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree that under these items at the bottom, 1, 2, and 3, in item 1 a cease-fire in Kosovo is envisaged, a cessation of hostilities. Item 2 envisages an improvement of humanitarian situation and averting the impending humanitarian catastrophe, and a third point deals with the political solution to the Kosovo crisis. Do you agree this is the essence of these three points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't got it on my screen, but that's the essence, yes. Sorry, I have it, I was looking somewhere else. This is why, of course, 1199 was superseded by Resolution 1203 in which the -- two of the documents were actually incorporated, in answer to your earlier question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When was the 1203 adopted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember on Friday I had a little piece of paper that you wouldn't let me use. I had actually written down the actual date of the Resolution 1203, but it was -- it mentions both -- it mentions both of the Clark-Naumann and the Geremek Agreement to be, sort of, incorporated into the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I agree, that's probably right, but that is after the period relevant to the indictment. During the break, please have a look and tell us after the break the date of the 1203 Resolution. Thank you for this answer. Now, below this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at para 4 on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at item 4(a), the language there, and then I'd like to ask you ... Does it demand cessation of all action by the security forces affecting the civilian population and orders the withdrawal of security units only used for civilian repression, only those units that are in contact with civilians? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't use the word "only," but it says: "... withdrawal of security units used for civilian repression."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Right. But the other party to the conflict, the KLA, is not mentioned anywhere, no measures are envisaged in application to them; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the problems of the agreement. This actually was, if you like, one-sided. But reference had been made, I remember in the Geremek Agreement and possibly in 1199 also, somewhere else, that actually asked both sides to abide by the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will briefly go through to all these documents. But this first one, I did not have on Friday and that's why I started with it. Also, it preceded the others. Witness, under items -- sub-items (b) and (c), we can read the provisions about verification, about the return of refugees, and the need to establish dialogue. Now, in para 5, item (d), I would like your comment. Is it right that sub-item (d) concerns measures against peaceful population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, item (d) says: "Unimpeded access to humanitarian organisations and humanitarian supplies."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand me. Sub-item (b).

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the question, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Item (b) also concerns only the civilian population, not the KLA, the other party to the armed conflict; am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call now for the next page, para 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, it is the FRY that is primarily responsible for the security of the mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Whatever happens to any member of the mission, Yugoslavia would be responsible and Yugoslavia has to take steps to ensure your security because you, the verifiers, were unarmed; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And we'll come back to that again later. At the initiative of the KVM sometime towards March, just before you left, an agreement was made that with your consent, in areas affected by conflict with terrorists, you would enter such areas once you signed away Yugoslavia's responsibility, you do it at your own risk; correct? I think it was on the 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at para 11. Does this paragraph relate to the financing of the KLA and their gathering of funds to buy arms and bring them into Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, but that's what I would assume it to mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's why you're a diplomat. Tell me now, did Albania and other countries comply with these provisions of the resolution? During your tenure in Kosovo and Metohija, what was the situation with the supply of arms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were aware that arms were being smuggled across the border from Albania into Kosovo, mainly because, you know, every time the Serbian security forces captured the -- had a confrontation with the smugglers, we were told, so we knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And there were several cases involving you once of border incidents on the border with Albania when 35 men got killed during an attempt to illegally enter with weapons. Can you say your answer for the record?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you say that I was involved, I wasn't involved in the operation of smuggling the weapons, but I was certainly aware that this had happened because we were informed. And later I was also instrumental in dealing with the prisoners who were held in the prison in Nis, those who had survived the ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned D00160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us skip a few documents and go to P838.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember where we left off on Friday?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Judge Parker asked me at a quarter to 2.00 whether I still have questions for you in cross-examination because we were at the end of our session. I said, Yes; and he seemed surprised. He said, I just asked. Now, about this letter of the 23rd September addressed to Mr. Milosevic by Mr. Walker. I'll get to the point straightaway. You were a continuation of KDOM, and while you were getting settled and starting to work, the agreements were being implemented, the three agreements that we mentioned that you said were your Bible.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, I mean, to get the mission going there had to be concurrent activity. So, for example, the mission was being set up in early October, ambassadors being appointed in October, I think the 17th of October, Ambassador Walker was appointed well before the official date the mission started. Preparatory work and teams were going out to Kosovo and Belgrade to work out where the mission would be best placed and how to operate it. Documents were being written ahead of the mission starting its day-to-day work because you had to do this in order to start the mission. So there was a lot of preparatory work which had to be done to get the mission going as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best, but please answer this question: My question was, Before the KVM was formed, the Kosovo diplomatic mission took a certain position on these three agreements and decided whether the FRY was applying them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know. I don't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know. You know why I'm asking? Because from the moment when the agreements were activated until you arrived, more than a months elapsed; and there are certain document that I thought you were familiar with because the KDOM were supposed to hand over, and, I understood, handed over to you all the documentary evidence about the application of these three agreements from the beginning. Now, about this letter, you were not in Kosovo or in Yugoslavia when it was written, and that's the reason I asked you this, because this letter refers to certain questions that had already been settled with KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up P836.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is the agreement dated 25th October, 1998, between Mr. Byrnes and Djordjevic. Please look at para 2. Do you agree that this paragraph envisages that in case of incidents or increased tension, the police will have the right to perform patrol duties in armoured vehicles equipped with machine-guns up to 7.9 millimetres on the condition of notifying the KDOM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, regarding para 3, is it correct that the FRY complied with the provisions of para 3 and withdrew its forces from Dragobilje, Ostrozub, Opterusa, Dobrodeljane, Studencani, Samodraza, Pecane, and Klecka?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that they complied with paragraph 2 and 3, I don't remember but you can ask others like DZ later whether in fact the paragraph says "... upon notifying KDOM/OSCE ..." I'm not sure this notification was ever given. In answer to your second part of the question, I believe that those stationary forces were removed from those areas you mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness kindly speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that all these areas that the forces of the FRY abandoned were occupied by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was normal for the -- [B/C/S/ on English channel]. Sorry, yes, it was normal for the KLA to actually pull out -- to replace any VJ or MUP positions upon the withdrawal of the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that a violation of the agreement, regardless of the fact that the KLA was not a signatory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's considering they weren't a signatory, then they probably weren't violating anything, were they? Morally, yes, they were in violation because there should have been a cease-fire, but legally they hadn't signed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I must say that this opinion of yours is very interesting. The FRY, by complying with the agreement, enables the KLA to occupy territories it did not have, and that is called "complying." But if the FRY tries to stop that from happening, despite a cease-fire, then it is in violation of the agreement; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we ever said that -- that the VJ and the MUP would have no right to defend themselves or the population if the KLA were actually posing any danger to the locals. The fact that they were occupying land that was being vacated by the Serbian forces, as long as it was done peacefully, had no bearing on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, both in your statements and in other evidence I found that the KLA considered it a provocation when in Dragobilje or some other village patrol of the army or the police were patrolling as usual and they would then shoot at the vehicles --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the KVM considered it a provocation when the army or the police were patrolling in villages and then the KLA would shoot at them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more than a provocation, and these Serb security forces had every reason and right to take retaliatory action. But if they were sitting in a position which they had occupied and not bothering anybody, then that's a different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's take the notorious event in Dulje. The police forces were performing regular patrol duty, and they were bothering the KLA which launched an attack, but that was not what I wanted to say. I enumerated certain areas from which the Yugoslav forces withdraw, and the KLA then took control of these areas. They considered it a provocation when a patrol passed through, and they would attack them. And to that you would say that the Yugoslav forces were in violation and the KLA were not responsible for anything because -- and they were not violating anything, because they were not a signatory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't support that premise. What I was saying is that the Serbian forces, I'll repeat, had every right to retaliate against any attack upon them or upon the people the Serbian people in Kosovo; and I would also add that the OSCE, the KVM, we spent a lot of time trying to persuade the KLA not to occupy these positions and get off these position. And in fact we had some success in the area of Podujevo where we did keep the KLA a certain distance away and got them to relinquish some of the positions which they had taken overlooking the main road. So we tried pretty hard to keep the KLA out of these positions because we knew what the response would be and what action it would provoke.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphones. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's make a little digression now. I understood that the Kosovo Verification Mission based its work on reports and observations that were put on paper through which you informed the head of your mission and other agencies, if necessary; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, when wasn't it possible for you to write down in your reports whatever you observed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was in the field and I was staying out in the field, I wasn't able to come back and submit a report. Or there was so much going on that it was virtually impossible to, sort of, write everything down, and quite often my reports would be just verbal reports by telephone, by satellite telephone, by verbal debrief back at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you come back to the headquarters, didn't you have time to put down on paper whatever you had telephoned before or notified verbally and submitted to the fusion cell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's accept that in cases of emergency and in certain other situations when you simply couldn't do it, you did not submit reports, but these were exceptions rather than the rule; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think most of my work was done verbally in the field where I was just used, as I said before, as a firefighter, someone who would go out and try and resolve a problem in the field. And I would report back usually in verbal form because there were only so many hours in a day, and we were already working 18 hours a day if not more sometimes, seven days a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if you are in the field and you are unable to report, the person you informed, the headquarters in Pristina would pass it on in some material form, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What used to happen, I would go back -- come back, if I was back in Pristina, I would go to the fusion cell, then I would debrief the people in the fusion cell as to what had happened, and what had been done, et cetera; and they would then incorporate it into their reports directly from my comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you said in your statement something about the verification of police check-points, despite all the effort and all the documents that I had at my disposal, verification in the February of 1999 is something I haven't been able to find anywhere.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't mean you don't have a copy of it. I don't keep copies. But the report was written, I'm not sure whether I signed it or one of my subordinates had signed it because I might have been doing something else, but it was a long detailed report of exactly where all the check-points had been found, the observation posts, who had visited them, and it was a detailed report that was put in. Might not be under my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I wasn't even looking for a report under your name. This is the third time you are testifying. Did you use or show that report in the Milosevic trial or the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to it in the Milosevic and the Sainovic trial, but I don't have any documents with me. So the only documents would be the documents with the Court or with the various witnesses like DZ, for example, or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, you understand very well what I asked you. Please answer my question. Did you see the document, that report you just mentioned, in the Milutinovic case or in the Milosevic trial? I know it is not under -- I know your name is not on it, but it doesn't matter who authored it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the document, yes. Not in the court, but I've seen it in Kosovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the courtroom. Did you see it, perhaps, on Friday, last Friday in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There might have been reference to it, but I did not see the actual report, no. I don't believe I saw it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have here a chronology of events from the operations HQ where you worked where it says that on the 5th of January, 1999 - that's para 58, Exhibit 65 ter 634, page 353 in English. On the 5th of January, an inspection was carried out of all MUP observation points, and in the comments it says "Mainly used by MUP ." This is dated the 5th of January. Is it possible that this is the report, the event you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you see that in the comments there is no mention of any violation, do you agree? Have you seen -- do you see this document now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I called up document 65 ter P634, if we can see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I was just going to ask for the document to be called up, since the screen was blank - but I see now that it has appeared - that it would aid all parties to have it available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page B-3, item 58.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see it. It says: "All 27 OPs inspected. Most occupied by MUP." Which implies that there was a violation because only 9 should have been occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you do agree it was the 5th of January?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, DZ was very meticulous with his paperwork, so this is one of his pieces of work, so I wouldn't disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if this is the correct translation, but what I see, "Mainly used by MUP" in my version. I don't know if this is the correct translation. Most. Most.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't -- it means that most of the -- of the OPs were occupied by the MUP. That means nearly all, "most" as in "nearly all." That's the correct translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 65 ter 659.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are not tendering that report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told it's part of P844, already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we'll have a problem with the admission of this -- of some of the evidence because some exhibits have been admitted more than once, but it's good that this one is already in evidence, because I was going to use it again and I thought I would tender it; but if it's already exhibited, that's even better. Now I'd like 659 from the 65 ter list. That's the daily report for the 4th and 5th of January, 1999. I am sorry, I apologise to the legal officer, it's D156.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at this report for the period up to the 5th of January, and then read para 1, the first passage in para 1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says: "Not all OPs were manned." Full details will be to follow. "Not all" means "most." "Possibly" could mean "most."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is contrary to what you've just said, that there were violations. How come when not all were even manned, what kind of violation is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already said on numerous occasions that the agreement, Byrnes agreement, said that one-third of the 27 should be manned at the most, and there were, that means 9 should have been manned. The other report, DZ 's annex, shows that most were maned. This says that not all OPs were manned, which means that there's no number on it, but it's not all. But it's closer to all than not any. Also, there were other OPs that had been set up on top of the 27 but there's a report to follow. The report's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Nobody has seen that report. You are just telling us about it, but we can't find a document about it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in addition, there are the -- you can see there on the second line of that first sentence, it says: "Full details of the verification are contained in the individual regional centre daily reports." From which the -- we have to get those documents first to then produce the main report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me then, where is that main report containing your assertions? That's what I'm saying. What you are saying is not backed by documents, and what is written here is contrary to what you said, not even to mention the fact that this is a completely different period, a month before.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said it before, you know, if you read the English, you can actually understand what it says. It says that most were manned, which means most of the 27 were manned. This one says not all OPs were manned, which confirms what the other statement made. And where the report is, I do not know. I'm not a custodian of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate it very much if you would read out to us the English version of the first paragraph in item 1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "Verification (2/99) of all the 27 MUP OPs were conducted today. Not all OPs were manned."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on, and the Court will make its own judgement. While we are still discussing verification, in item 58 we see on the 4th of January an inspection was carried out of three approved positions of the combat team. Do you agree this refers to the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And again, there is no observation about a violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe there were any violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But tell me now, I don't understand one thing, if your main activity was verification and if you establish that a certain agreement or part of that agreement is not complied with, isn't that a reason to make a protest and tell the Commission for Cooperation, Look here, such an such provision of the agreement is being violated, please do something about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that following the inspection of the MUP points, observation check-points, this issue was raised at the Cooperation Commission in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, if such a document existed, I would show it to you and then ask my question. It's not in the chronology, and it's nowhere in the documents that the police or the army were responsible for any violations; and there is no such document until the very end of your tenure in Kosovo. There's only one towards the end of December when DZ tried to enter the barracks of the Pristina Corps and he wasn't allowed in, and he wrote in his report that he wasn't allowed in. There were no further assertions of any violations. Would it be right that this is -- this can be explained by the fact that you changed your method of work, you wrote down the numbers of lorries and tanks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please put a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He has done that. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it was because we changed our method of work at all. I mean, I don't know where the documents are. As I said to you before, there were so many documents, a lot of them have been archived, some people have them in their possession, a lot of documents were destroyed on our, sort of, departure from Kosovo. We spent three days shredding paperwork in the OSCE building in Kosovo. Just looking at the question...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was it a change in your method of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That caused the -- well, I mean, we were adapting our method of work continuously, but that wouldn't have been the reason that this wouldn't have been reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, there is evidence that all that was done in Kosovo and Metohija by the KVM was transferred on disks to Macedonia during withdrawal and what was not necessary was destroyed. All this documentation that I'm showing to you, I got from the Prosecution and from the OSCE. So these are not private documents. But I'm telling you, we have information from this chronology that on the 20 something December, General DZ went to the barracks of the Pristina Corps and he wasn't allowed in. And he also went once to Pristina to General Delic's office, he was allowed in and had a discussion. Those are the only two instances of application of Mrs. Phelan's method that I could notice, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entry into the barracks General -- into Colonel Delic's barracks was not Mrs. Phelan's method, it was more the diplomatic way of entering the barracks, when we were invited in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You probably mean some later instance. This is hardly one I'm talking about, but never mind. I have more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up P835. It is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is the Geremek-Jovanovic Agreement. First of all, I'd like to focus on item 3. These are the general provisions, but under Roman III there is something I'd like to look at. Am I right in saying that the special mandate was for members to maintain a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the -- it wasn't our mandate to maintain a cease-fire. It was our mandate to verify the cease-fire. We had no way to enforce a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, but the translation I have says: "The Verification Mission shall travel throughout Kosovo to check whether all the participants are maintaining the cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't got it on my screen. I only have the first line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That should be also page -- English page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's now on the screen. The problem is, the paragraph has a line at the bottom of one page and then continues on the next. You have the second page now. Do you have a point about this paragraph, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I want to say that the agreement envisages that you travelled throughout Kosovo, not that you should inspect the military installations and barracks of the Army of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you are now going to ask the witness if that is his understanding of the paragraph; is that correct? Yes, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Well, it says that we have to verify the maintenance of the cease-fire by all elements, and reports -- investigate reports of cease-fire violations. But it continues with other phrases that, you know, we are to be able to look at -- if you take all the other agreements into consideration, we are checking if the weapons of the 12.7 millimetres are around, if everybody is back in barracks, and so on. When it says "freedom of movement and access" if it said "freedom of movement" that means moving around Kosovo, which we had. Access means access. It means the entrance into places that we wish to go into in order to verify all aspects of the cease-fire. And all aspects of the cease-fire are compliance with all the agreements and you can only do that by going into barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think I raised two problems, but since it's time for the break, I'd like -- I'll put these two questions after the break. It's time, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will continue after the normal break at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, we were still with the Geremek-Jovanovic agreement, and I said that two issues have opened up. The first one is the issue of interpretation -- interpreting the agreement. Not only at your level. I also realise that there were issues at other levels such as the level of General Drewienkiewicz and Mr. Walker. Did you ever try to raise that issue to the level of the presiding officer of the OSCE and the Yugoslav president in order to deal with the issue of the way the verification agreement should be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why Ambassador Walker wrote the letter to Mr. Milosevic spelling out exactly how the system would work, and it was mentioned endlessly at meetings of access and verification at the meetings we had between General DZ and General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question. Mr. Walker drafted a letter in November. You had problems in December with verification, that issue included DZ and Mr. Walker later on. Did you try to raise the issue with some higher instances such as the Presidency of the OSCE and the Yugoslav Presidency in order to deal with the problem of agreement interpretation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that General DZ wrote letters to the OSCE, raised the issue on many occasions as I don't know for fact, but I understand that Ambassador Walker did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The other issue is this: We touched upon this question, but we haven't completed it, KDOM as of the moment the agreement was signed, conducted Verification Missions until the KVM was formed. In the the month and a half they were in charge of verifying whether the FRY was meeting the conditions of the agreement, transfer weapons, warehousing of equipment, whether the weapons were being brought out into fields, and various other issues; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 3 of the agreement, that is to say, item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, am I right in saying that police forces had the right to set up check-points in order to control traffic or to control and prevent crime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the act of illegally possessing a fire-arm is a criminal offence in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Smuggling of different types of goods which are of limited supply, drugs, all those are offences. Why do you believe that setting up check-points in that regard without discrimination, that is to say that all persons passing through such check-points would be subjected to checks, would that be a violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the agreement actually said we should be notified of any such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But the issue at hand are security in placements and we had check-points and crime control points. This is regular traffic control and crime control, why would you need to be notified of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just says -- I mean, I'm just reading from the document: "We will receive notification should circumstances lead to a establishment of a roadblock other than for traffic or crime control." It's very difficult to differentiate between what the purpose of your roadblock is. And that's the difficulty; this is where the difficulty came in. Is the roadblock purely to look for people smuggling cigarettes, or is it something else? Is it to make the life of the people intolerable?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I fully agree that it is difficult, but according to the agreement, such controls, such check-points were allowed, and you did not need to be notified. I believe the only criterion that was to be applied was that there was -- they were placed indiscriminately irrespective of people's ethnicity, and that the purpose of such check-points was to exercise control without prejudice.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, that's a statement. Do you want an answer from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do expect an answer. I'm asking you whether you agree that as regards traffic checks and crime control, the Verification Mission did not need to be notified pursuant to para 3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to para 3 that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move to para 4 concerning the borders. There were also interpretation problems whether that needed to be notified or not. First we need to see what your interpretation was of the border belt of 5 kilometres. Was the Verification Mission allowed to enter the 5 kilometre border belt without prior notification?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yes because the Verification Mission had access and freedom of movement. This paragraph refers to visiting border controlled units and accompanying them on the normal border control roles. It doesn't say anything about us actually going into the border belt, which as you well know at one point became as wide as 15 kilometres and grew wider by the day as the end of March came closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with that, but I think it at times was as large as 10 kilometres. In any case, let us go back to para 4. It says: "... through areas of Kosovo away from the border." That is the end of the first sentences. This para concerns the areas away from the border.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't talk about access, it say that we will maintain liaison about border control activities away from the border. Nothing about access.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but look at the next sentence, that such missions will be conducted when invited by the FRY authorities or upon its request. Therefore, there must have been a request. There should have been for you to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a request was required from either side. However, it does say: "... to visit border control units and to accompany them on their normal border patrols." But the border belt, as you say, was enormous and so you couldn't prevent us entering the border belt to see what was going on. We went always looking to accompany patrols. I didn't write these rules, and I didn't -- I didn't, sort of, screw up the meaning of these -- of what was actually meant. Unfortunately, many agreements are writing very badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You just commented on the second part of the sentence, whereas the initial part, the first part of the sentence it is stated that the mission needed to be invited by the authorities or upon its request. Therefore a request must precede a verification visit, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A visit to a border control unit is the answer given in the beginning. Mr. Djurdjic, I am getting increasingly concerned at the time you are taking. You've got points to make. They can be made far much quicker than they are. You've got a point here to make about paragraph 4, you've made it. The witness has given his comment which disagrees with your interpretation. No further questions are going to change that. Move on to the next point, please, or we'll be spending the whole day with this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very well. I thought and believe that the witness was interpreting the provisions fairly. In any case, I leave it up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let us move on, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will no longer need this document. Could we please have P837 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is the Clark-Naumann agreement of the 25th October, 1998. Do you agree with me that the gist of this agreement was basically the communique issued by the federal government in terms of its obligations that it had undertaken? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should move on to the communique itself. That is page 3 in the English. The Roman numeral III, last sentence: "However, state authorities as the last measure in keeping with the principle of self-defence retain the right to respond appropriately and adequately to any type of terrorist activity and breaking the law, endangering the lives of citizens, and security of a state body's employees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not able to see the reference in the agreement that Defence counsel is referring to on the screen. I think it will assist us to have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the court clerk to show us the Roman numeral III. It's the last sentence. It's the last page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of this and the only thing that doesn't apply is the word "proportionately."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where do you find the word "proportionately"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "... the State authorities retain the right to respond adequately and proportionately to any form of terrorist activity or violation of law, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Was this the basis that the FRY forces could be employed when terrorist activities occur and when the KLA jeopardized the lives and safety of civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned proportionality. Did you ever see a single protest that was sent to the Yugoslav authorities because there was a disproportionate use of force? Did you ever see such a document sent by Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. But I know it was -- we preached this concept of proportionality at almost every meeting we had with the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we said it was only Mr. Walker who could decide, following consultations with you, what a violation was and that it was he who could forward a protest on behalf of the KVM; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Or a delegated member of his team could, yes, on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for document P -- I think this is a 65 ter document. 00677. Although, I'm pretty sure it was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You will recall this document, Witness. Yes, this is it. It says 1(a) "Prizren District."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you read out the part of the sentence or the sentence that begins with "EUAG." Just that one single sentence out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "EUAG observed several armed civilians. An OSCE patrol reported a shooting in the village. Two dead male bodies and a wounded woman were found. Details to follow."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That suffices. First of all, can you tell us what the acronym EUAG stands for, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at this a few times, and I just cannot at all, unless it observes to -- refers to some sort of EU mission that was based in Belgrade. I have no idea. An unknown acronym to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that KLA members also operated in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and they didn't really have a uniform as such, the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What conclusion do you arrive at based on this formulation when it says the EUAG observed several armed civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible to tell from this whether it refers to Serb or Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday, when the Prosecutor asked you about this, you said that this referred to some Serbs. That is why I was asking you this since there was no indication as to who it referred to, and we didn't see any evidence of that. In any case, thank you. Could you tell me something about the acronym SITCEN, what does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the situation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whose situation centre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is the reference to this, sorry, so I can see what context it's mentioned in?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is in the context of the OSCE report. It says to be delivered to the deputy head of mission and Mr. DZ, and then it says SITCEN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We can have that placed on the screen at this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Djurdjic please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is document 65 ter 00650, last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the record, the last document the witness commented on was Exhibit P839.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise, the previous document was P389.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 839, yes. Could we please have the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This says distribution. From the top, the second abbreviation is SITCEN.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Sorry. I would have initially guessed that the situation centre would have been the fusion centre, but there must be another organisation that slipped my mind completely. The situation centre is an organisation, I presume, within the OSCE that monitored the current situation. I thought it was the fusion cell, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was it perhaps the situation centre of the NATO staff or headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have NATO as one of our places that we distributed our documents to, so I thought it would have said NATO's SITCEN or saying similar, but it doesn't say that. I don't believe that we sent anything to NATO like this. Also, these -- this would be an internal distribution, otherwise it would say external distribution as well. So if it's just distribution, it insinuates it's an internal distribution. Only these people within the organisation, the headquarters of the OSCE, would receive it; liaison, current ops, fusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you are familiar with the statement of Mr. Afrim Aziri from the previous cases. Can you tell me what jobs, what tasks this Mr. Afrim Aziri performed for the KVM while he was in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Aziri was originally General DZ's driver, and then he became my driver for tasks basically around Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you enabled him to receive KLA fax messages via your friends who were in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that Mr. Aziri helped us with was before we left, he spent some time giving me the plan and the information of how the airfield -- military airfield in Pristina was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the time after the 24th that you enabled him to receive fax messages from the KLA in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking now about the time after the mission had left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, having -- in the last -- in the Milutinovic et al. trial I've been show the letter that Mr. Aziri had written. I've already commented on this. And I had nothing to do with any fax messages or anything he was doing for anyone while he was sitting in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know whether he was in contact with Mr. David Meyer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Afrim was always trying to do something to help the KLA, and I mean, we had -- we used to sit and have coffee together in one of the hotels in Macedonia, Afrim and David Meyer, and myself, and a few others; and Afrim kept -- often would talk about trying to do something to help the KLA. But we had no need of that type of help because we had our own ways of finding out what was happening in Kosovo after we had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us about this own way you had of receiving information about developments in Kosovo after the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, NATO had its own people in Kosovo throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you mean inside the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, NATO had its own, as anyone would -- I mean, it's a normal thing you do when you are carrying out a campaign or a bombing campaign you're going to carry out later on, you'd have somebody on the ground, if you can, one of our own highly trained NATO soldiers, nothing to do with the OSCE, who would be actually providing targeting data for NATO, observing what is on the ground. Isn't that what good armies do?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: They certainly do, but through forces on the ground, not through their own soldiers. But do you know if there was a direct contact between the KLA headquarters and NATO forces in Macedonia and Albania?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I mean, I was attached as a liaison officer by the OSCE to NATO. I wasn't part of the NATO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but I asked not about yourself, but in general terms. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know about that. I mean, I wasn't in a position to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what was the substance of your function as KVM in Macedonia after the war started, after the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had several functions. I was work along with the UNHCR and making sure -- looking at the refugees and helping the refugees, helping set up the camps. I was also as -- in my liaison function between NATO and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am sorry, I have to interrupt you. I'm interested exclusively in your connection with NATO. I know from your statement about what you did, but I'm interested in the connection between the KVM and NATO and exactly what was the job of the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day I attended a NATO briefing along with other NGOs where I was able to take notes of what was going on in general with a mission, the operation, and I was able to put questions as well if we had any questions about building refugee camps, helping refugees, and so on. It was not a military activity. It was a coordinating activity. As at that time, NATO was spending a lot of its time building refugee camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At the same time it was bombing Yugoslavia. And you, as a member of the KVM, an international organisation, were communicating with the organisation that was at war with the FRY?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was attending briefing meetings in the morning. I don't know what you mean I was communicating or collaborating with the -- with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked you to explain to me the substance of that connection. But tell me, who was the liaison officer? Who was liaising within the KVM with the authorities of Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was one contact between the OSCE mission in Macedonia when I think I wrote a letter or, I spoke on the telephone to General Loncar about something, I can't remember what it was, but I don't think there was very much negotiation at our level. If there was negotiation going on, it would have been at the Vienna level, not at our level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm only talking about the KVM, the Verification Mission, not the Vienna level or the higher levels of the OSCE. I'm talking about the same level on which you were communicating on a daily basis with NATO. Did anyone on behalf of the KVM in Macedonia or Albania communicate on a daily basis with the authorities of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the documentation that I have, in your work you also communicated with Mr. Kotur?
