utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember recognising on the footage, the equipment and weapons belonging to the KLA? Equipment bearing a visible emblem of the FBI, on caps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which footage? There was a -- I have a vague memory of seeing somebody once with a -- someone in the KLA with an FBI hat, but I can't remember where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That was in Pristina, if I may remind you, at the meeting with Mr. Kotur.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what was the footage? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I suppose it was actually photographs that were shown to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. There is a vague memory of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember the comment, that the message of the photo was clear in view of that emblem?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: The witness has already said that he only has a vague memory of these photographs, and he is now being asked further questions about the photograph in question. I wonder if it's possible for Defence counsel to show the witness the photograph in order to aid him in answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have the photograph. I've just reminding the witness of a conversation about that photograph. He said he had a vague memory, and I am asking him whether he remembered the conclusion of that conversation, if he remembers what he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the conversation, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ciaglinski and Mr. Kotur. I've already said that, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you putting to the witness that he had a conversation with Mr. Kotur in which it was suggested that the presence of an FBI hat was sending a very clear message? Is that what you are putting?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only asked if he remembered something like that being said as a conclusion when he was shown the photograph. He said he remembered vaguely the photograph, now I'm asking if he remembers the conclusion. I'm not trying to influence the witness. I'm just asking if he recalls it or not, and then maybe later I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are obscuring completely, as far as I'm concerned at the moment what you are at, but perhaps, Colonel, you can help us. Do you remember any comment about a hat in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't. I could probably try and sort of put a meaning on to it now, but I'm not sure if that's the meaning that would have applied at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your own interpretation or imagination is not something we are searching for today. There you are, Mr. Djurdjic. Now, do you want to move on from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. I just tried to jog the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you brought back some, or rather, sent back some verifiers because they were reporting in a biased way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't, but I believe that a number of verifiers were sent home for being biased, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, when I'm asking you these questions about the mission, I know that you did not personally work in administration, but I'm asking you about some personal knowledge that you may perhaps have. I don't mean to imply that it was part of your own duties.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you be so kind as to tell us something about your visit to Decani on the 15th of January and what happened there, who were you with and what happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite a long story, but I'll try to make it shorter. The actual plan was that on the -- on that date, the VJ -- sorry, the MUP were going to exchange personnel at a forward observation post between Decani and Jablanica and this was well inside what the KLA considered to be their territory. And to ensure the safety of the personnel of the MUP, they were going to be supported quite heavily with VJ and other assets. And this looked as if it was going to become quite ugly, and it could have turned up -- turned into another confrontation, armed confrontation. And so I spent the entire day negotiating with the MUP and with the KLA, with Ramush Haradinaj, personally, to ensure that this thing went smoothly and try to explain to everyone that it wasn't a reinforcement but it was a exchange of personnel and the status quo would remain the same. All went well until we actually tried to do the procedure. After driving down this track for a few of kilometres, two of my vehicles were leading, I was in the second vehicle, and we were followed by a truck with a MUP personnel in it, and behind me I had another vehicle belonging to the KVM. And unfortunately we came under fire. We were attacked and two of my personnel were wounded. And it transpired that the firers were not Serb, but they were actually KLA fighters who had a personal grudge against the OSCE. I think originally, it was incorrectly reported as an attack by Serbian forces, but that was later corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up Exhibit 65 ter 00637. Second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, is this a press release by the KLA regarding this incident of the 15th of January, you just discussed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I now call up 65 ter 00638.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is another press release regarding the events of the 8th of January at Dulje. Can you tell me what you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think basically what it says on the press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that? Were you informed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, so it was just what I read and what I had heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does this press release reflect what you heard at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, and we, I mean, Colonel Mijatovic -- whenever there was such an attack took place would come to the meetings in the morning at 10.00 and brief me about these incidents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call for 65 ter 00643.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know and were you involved in an incident of hostage-taking by the KLA on the 8th of January in Stari Trg?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure I heard about it, but I don't think I was involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 3 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It says: 10.05 "Lieutenant-Colonel Ciaglinski called up DZ to inform that verifiers were on the ground only 5 minutes away from VJ positions."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I need to read, I mean, I haven't seen this document for some time, if ever. You threw this thing at me, I can't remember immediately if I was there, involved, knew about it, read about it. Is this the incident where the VJ soldiers were captured? Is this the one? Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It has to do with the eight soldiers.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I remember now, yes, sorry, I was involved, quite closely, intimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And I see that you informed General DZ at least twice because you were on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that this document be also admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00163, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to refresh your memory now about these inspections of border areas. Do you remember that, among other things, you spoke to Mr. Tomislav Mladenovic on the Yugoslav side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: According to my information, he was deputy head of the coordination team of the federal government in Pristina. Did you have a meeting with him on the 18th of January regarding border inspections and that this gentleman, or perhaps someone else you don't remember by name, warned you that verifiers were still coming to the border area without prior notification, and he said that every such visit needed to be notified in advance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had several such meetings, so it's -- what you are saying almost certainly happened, but exactly with whom and what date, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the information I have, you replied that you had your instructions about the procedure for border inspections and that you had agreed a joint inspection with Colonel Kotur, which inspection had been postponed because of the kidnapping of VJ soldiers, and you were engaged personally in attempts to free them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that on that occasion you said you were visiting KLA prisoners in jail in Nis, and that you were satisfied with the way they were treated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: The witness is being referred to previous information, occasions that he spoke or information that the Defence counsel has. I wonder if it will assist if the source of such information is provided, whether it's a document or statement of prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Clearly, Ms. Gopalan is at a disadvantage trying to pick up if there is a reference to these incidents, Mr. Djurdjic. You are simply asking the witness whether he recalls something. If you have a particular documentary reference, it would help if you could give that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have my notes of the conversation, that's why I'm not showing them. I'm asking the witness if he remembers the conversation. The notes originate from third persons, and I'm just asking the witness to confirm whether something is correct or not. What I have are notes, not witness statements, so I can't use them with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, that clarifies the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We discussed something on Friday, and I told you I found a reference in your documents to the fact that you prepared several times for evacuation from the FRY. And in something written by Mr. Wilson, I read the recommendation to all verifiers that they should have a suitcase packed at every -- at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up now D003-0860.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you know this document. It's dated 22nd January, 1999, and it concerns plans for evacuation of Kosovo verifiers from Kosovo. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mm-hmm. I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank God at that time there was no need for an evacuation; right? On the 22nd of January. You remained in the territory of Kosova and Metohija. Generally speaking, were you happy with your withdrawal when you made decisions on it on the 17th and the 20th? And I have in mind the way you were treated by FRY forces during your withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's relevant of, you know, what the situation at the time is. Every international organisation has to have a withdrawal plan from any theatre. Recently in Georgia, nobody was threatening us, but we had a plan to withdraw and how we would withdraw from Georgia as a mission if we had to. The situation was degenerating things were becoming more difficult, and we believed that it was imperative to have an evacuation plan that everybody was happy with and prepared for, so -- because if the -- once the evacuation was announced, should it be necessary, then it had to happen very quickly, within hours, not within days or weeks. And we're not dealing with, I told you before, purely military personnel on this mission, there are a lot of the personnel were civilians who had very little experience with missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, while you were in Kosovo until the 24th, do you know of any situations in which certain villages were vacant of their Albanian population because that population had joined the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that you are very familiar with Kosova and Metohija during the relevant time, could you tell me this: Where was the focus of all activity in Kosovo, and I don't mean the Verification Mission, but the forces of the FRY and KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were certain pockets, as you well know, of activity, there was a pocket in Podujevo; and to the west of it, there would have been pockets in Stimlje, there would have been Orahovac, I mean, all over the place there were pockets, Jablanica where Haradinaj had his headquarters. That was a little area to the -- not exactly Jablanica because that's where he was, but on the peripheries of that area. So yes, there were many areas where the KLA had activity and the VJ and MUP had an interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that for the most part activities took place in the villages?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where most of the damage and fighting took place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for me the yard of a typical countryside Albanian home?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends if you are talking about one of the larger homes with a wall around it and a number of dwellings inside. But normally there were animals, there were haystack, wood piled up, hay piled up. Animals, pigs, chickens -- no pigs, chickens. What else would you like?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that. I'm interested in the walls. What were the walls made of and of what height were they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they varied a lot but, I mean, some of the bigger properties had quite tall walls, over 2 metres, and quite solid. I never personally examined the wall to see if it was made of rocks or mud, but I was aware that the walls were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your preparations to go to Kosovo, were you told anything about the percentages of Albanian population in the country-side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by country-side, but we were told where major population areas were, and these were mainly rural people, agricultural people living off the land, so we knew that they were all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you recall that in February 1999 - and whether you were familiar with it - that there was an incident between Lipovica and Magore which is 20 kilometres from Pristina, a police column was ambushed by the KLA during which 15 policemen were injured?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, vague recollections. I can't remember exactly. But the name Magore is somehow indelibly marked on my brain, so please reminds me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting with Colonel Kotur. He told you about it, and then you checked that over the phone and eventually confirmed his allegations. The verifiers confirmed that on the spot. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaguely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember notifying Mr. Kotur about the visit of Mr. Vollebaek, presiding officer of the OSCE? During that visit you also acquainted Mr. Vollebaek with the Serb position resulting in Mr. Kotur being satisfied with the information you shared with Mr. Vollebaek?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't remember exactly what was said or done. Again, I remember that there was the -- Vollebaek came occasionally, and I might have said something about this. I just can't remember that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember your position that it was possible that the KLA by provoking wanting to create conditions by a NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something I occasionally heard people discussing, that it would be in their interest to create a situation which would force someone else to intervene in the Kosovo crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that on that occasion you stated that Great Britain was not a KLA mentor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always said that, A, we had nothing to do with the KLA and didn't in any way sponsor it or their terrorism, but I also, I believe, mentioned that - and I said this on several occasions - that our defence minister at the time I think it was Lord Robertson said that the UK had no intention of sponsoring or supporting any NATO attack on Kosovo. So I said if you are considering doing this to entice NATO to come, you are barking up the wrong tree because we have no intention ever of -- well, not me personally, but our UK government has no intention of supporting a NATO action here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have D003-0867 next. This was not translated. In any case, I wanted to read out a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is an Official Note of a meeting held in Pristina on the 9th of February, 1999. In attendance was Richard Heaslip I think, if I'm pronouncing that right, and Major-General Sretan Lukic. Concerning what we have just discussed here, I wanted to say that on that occasion, General Lukic informed Mr. Heaslip that the police had information on the number of policemen at Kosovo that was forwarded to the American KDOM. Once the agreement was signed, they had a role in the OSCE, and they were also involved in the police withdrawal. They were also forwarded a patrol map of the police and the different check-points envisaged by the annex of the agreement, were you familiar with these facts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that meeting. I mean, that was a meeting I probably wasn't at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, there were many meetings, but I'm short on time and I cannot go through all of them. In any case, such meetings were held between representatives of the Kosovar Verification Mission and the police, and you were not in attendance. There must be 20 or 30 of them, however, I don't believe they are that important. Am I right in saying that other people from KVM had meetings with police representatives in Pristina and that you only attended those meetings which involved Mr. Loncar and the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I attended the meetings of the Cooperation Commission daily in Pristina, but I told you before in my evidence that there were meetings between the police, it was Guy Sands, I believe, originally he used to go and have meetings with the MUP; and later on February, March, I believe General Heaslip was talking to the MUP, yes. But the official organ of exchange of information was the Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My infallible associate just told me that I had wrong information and that indeed we do have a translation of this document. Therefore, I seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I take it you have more questions, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have some documents left. I'm going through the documents. I wanted to show them to the witness and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We must adjourn now for the second break, Mr. Djurdjic. You may continue after the break, but I hope you use the break to concentrate down to the matters that are important. There must be time for re-examination of this witness so that he finishes today. Thank you. We resume at 5 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, I have a procedural matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I should have raised this before the break, and I wasn't sufficiently speedy. My apologies for that. This is to do with the admission into evidence of D00165. And although it's been admitted, we would like to object to its admission simply because we believe that a sufficient basis hasn't been established for the document to be admitted into evidence. A part of it was read out. We subsequently were told that an English translation was available, but in terms of the witness's comments on the document, he said he wasn't aware of the meeting in question and that it wasn't a meeting that he probably attended. That would be his extent of information on that document which is not very much, and that would be the basis of our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll consider this as some later time. We want to be sure to finish the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I now call for Exhibit P841.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you recognise this photograph, you said it was your photograph. I'd like to ask you, What prevented you from filming such documents that we don't see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just -- it was a large presence of Serbian security forces, and I didn't really want to, sort of, annoy or upset people. I mean, to give you an example, I already had an experience around this time where I was threatened by some VJ soldiers with being shot just for being in the wrong place elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you expose yourself to danger when making this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What is your assessment of that documentation that was burnt? What kind of documents were they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all sorts. I took out several handfuls, and it was application forms, documents, passports, ID cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you, How come you were not afraid to take those IDs and you were afraid to make photos?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I went behind the vehicle where I couldn't be seen where I was taking those documents out of the pile of rubbish that was still there, that was smouldering. You couldn't see me. You notice if I step behind the vehicle, someone from the side here cannot see me. So I opened the back of the car, you know, to make it look as if I was doing something else, got a few handfuls of paper, and took them with me, put them in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you photograph them then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Because it was easier for me to just pick up some handfuls of stuff and put -- at the time I thought it was a good idea to just take some of the documents and put them in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that that building was supposed to be turned over to the successor of the KVM or KFOR, whoever?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand that certainly not the KVM - because the KVM went back into the original building, I believe, where the OSCE was before, which is up the road from this location - but I believe that some agreement had been made for NATO to use part of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it normal for archives that are no longer necessary to be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the KVM was evacuating from Pristina, did you destroy archived material that you didn't want to carry with you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We destroyed everything that, regardless of what it was, all paperwork was shredded except what we could take out with us on disks or hard drives. But for a different reason, it wasn't because it wasn't needed, it was impossible to carry it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a single document of those that you took away during any of the proceedings where you appeared as a witness?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean did I look at the documents that I took away? Yes, I did. And I discussed it with the interpreter who looked at the documents to tell me what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you, Were you shown any of those documents that you took away in the Milosevic trial or the Milutinovic trial, or in these past two days in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's stay on that period. You said you arrived after the 13th of June. Do you know how many Serbs left Kosovo after the NATO arrived in June 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thousands, I presume. I don't know exactly, but DZ and I spent a lot of our time going around Kosovo trying to persuade the Serbian population to remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were there any professional officers, professional policemen, who lived in Kosovo and worked there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. Of course there were professional policemen and soldiers who lived in Kosovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did they have to withdraw from Kosovo when the NATO forces arrived under the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't know, but I know that people like Colonel Kotur, who was a professional officer, was trying to get me to help him to retain his apartment in Kosovo. So I don't know if everybody in the VJ had to leave, including people who actually were living there normally. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I can't believe you don't know something like that. But let me tell you, under the agreement, all the troops and the police of the FRY had to leave Kosovo with a proviso that one day when the conditions are ripe, a thousand of them come back to the border. You said that troops and policemen were carrying looted property on their way out of Kosovo, how do you know that they were carrying looted property? How do you know that they were not carrying their own property as they would have had to leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I would have found it unlikely that virtually every vehicle that was leaving was covered in some sort of personal property. If what you are say is true, then a few of them would have been carrying personal possessions such as wardrobes, refrigerators, and so on. But not every vehicle. I mean, there were so many vehicles going out with this type of equipment strapped to the top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, they had to move their entire moveable property from Kosovo to Serbia, refrigerators, TV sets, furniture, depending on the type of vehicle they had. By the way, if you were on the border with Macedonia, didn't you see Albanians come in with truckfuls and tractorfuls of possessions when you were there in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that people who were leaving Kosovo at that time going to Macedonia, most of them came with nothing except a suitcase.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'd now like to come back to one incident you told us about when verifiers were mistreated at the border in contravention to the Vienna Agreement and the other covenants that were signed. Do you know that the FRY lodged in a protest to the mission because of the conduct of personnel at the border with Macedonia on the 25th and 26th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were accusations flying in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But would you agree with me that first in two out of three vehicles of the KVM there were no verifiers, only drivers who were Yugoslav nationals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we used local drivers, whether they were Albanians or Serbs. It was normal for the mission to use those sort of drivers. And it's normal in every embassy in the world that it's locals who are employed as drivers, but the vehicles still have diplomatic immunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you know very well what I said. Yugoslav nationals, regardless of ethnicity. But in those vehicles there were no members of the mission, whereas under the agreement at least one member of the KVM had to be in a KVM vehicle, the vehicle was not supposed to cross the border with just the driver in it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of such a regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the containers carried by those vehicles, there were no diplomatic markings. There was no proper inventory as envisaged by the Vienna Convention?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a cargo vehicle, then I can understand you talking about inventories, but ordinary diplomatic vehicles normally with diplomatic personnel in them don't require this type of inventory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And do you know that among other things those vehicles carried optical sights, a case for a pistol, chemical and other substances, and other equipment that were subject to declaration?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the pistol case being sent because there was always a discussion whether the body-guards for the ambassador or for senior members of the mission should be armed. And that was never allowed. And although this pistol case might have come, it's a leather pouch, but there was no pistol, and no one had arms. Chemicals, what chemicals? Are we talking about Sarin? I doubt. Maybe bleach or chemicals for photography or photocopiers, optical sights or binoculars? I don't know what you mean by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Regardless, medical and chemical substances must be declared at the border. In this specific case, the persons who were at the border did not do that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm pretty sure that if the vehicle is coming in with diplomatic personnel, and in the case of this - I know for a fact - in the case of this leather holster for the weapon, the diplomats, the KVM members, were actually in their vehicles. I don't believe it has to provide any inventory at all of what is in that vehicle. The vehicle is not subject to search.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the introductory part, I told you that two members of the Kosovo Verification Mission were in one vehicle, whereas the other two vehicles held no members of the mission, just Yugoslav drivers; and under the Vienna Convention, the goods in the vehicles needed to be declared, that's why a protest was lodged to the federal commission for the -- for cooperation of the FRY. Never mind. Do you know that on the 25th of February a KLA action to the south-west of Kacanik was noted and DZ put in his comment: "The first appearance of the KLA in this area."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, yes, something about this, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps the source of this comment could be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said chronology, item 112, 25th February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm interested in something else. This was just a reference. Can you explain why the KLA appeared in this area on the 25th of February, which was followed by a series of other incidents? I'm asking you as an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speculation again. There was a void, they were filling a void, an empty space that provided an opportunity. Kacanik is a strategically important area, obviously, so maybe that's the reason they might have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Kacanik canyon, the Kacanik gorge, is the only passage to the FRY and when NATO reaches Urosevac they need not stop before Belgrade anymore?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are assuming of course, that NATO was going to come through Kacanik, and it wasn't going to go straight from Kumanovo and straight up from that way. Much easier and less troublesome than going through a narrow gorge, if they are heading for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I was interpreted correctly. I meant when they were going from Macedonia when they passed the Kacanik gorge and reach Urosevac there are no more obstacles towards Belgrade and that would be the strategic path for NATO if an aggression occurs.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly one way of NATO entering, but it was the most dangerous and the one that would have caused the greatest number of casualties, and I believe NATO had other options as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know anything about Operation Arrow and the cooperation between the KLA and NATO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call for 6D -- sorry. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Ciaglinski, the meeting of the 5th of March with Colonel Ademovic at the MUP headquarters in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, vaguely again, but I need reminding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That was on the 5th of March. It had to do with the protest launched to the Verification Mission claiming that it obstructed passage on the road Pristina-Pec.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still no wiser at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And do you recall that on the 10th of March you spoke to Colonel Kotur and that you told him that in Kacanik and Ivaje some houses were damaged but that was far from what the KLA was claiming and what certain media reported? And you said there were witnesses on the ground who would deny such claims of the KLA in their reports.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question and my last document: 65 ter 00641. It's an evaluation of the KLA positions as of 15th March, 1999, by Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But that's not what I want to ask you. I'm interested in item 4(a). 4(a), do you see this passage: "In the course of preparations for the operation, brigade commander of the KLA for this area did not allow the UNHCR to evacuate displaced persons. This was interpreted as a cynical attempt to use Albanian civilians as human shields." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This is already an exhibit. I would in fact have a lot more to discuss with you, Colonel, but thank you for your answers. I must leave some time for the Prosecution as well. Thank you, Your Honours, for your patience. I have completed my cross-examination. May I just tender 65 ter 650.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which is that one? What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the document dated 26 February -- [in English] 26 February 1999 to 14 March 1999. Organisation for Security and Cooperation. [Interpretation] That's lines -- sorry, pages of the transcript 40 and 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The reference you have seems to be a document dated the 23rd of December, 1998. Is that the one that you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My infallible assistant is correcting me again. I was wrong. In any case, I don't want to take up any time. Let's leave this to Ms. Gopalan, and I will seek to tender this particular document through another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. You re-examine, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I have a few questions for you arising from Defence counsel's cross-examination. I'd first like to begin with document P839. In the interest of time, I don't think it's necessary to call up the document, but just to remind you, you were referred to a section in this document that spoke about armed civilians. That was in today's transcript at page 39, 16. And in response to Defence counsel's questions, you responded that from this reference in the document, it was impossible to tell if this reference was to Serbs or Albanians. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, taking a step back from this document, just speaking about armed civilians generally, you had testified last week about armed civilians whom you saw in Kosovo, and for the Court's reference, this is at page 5284. And just to remind you, you were asked about the arming of Serb civilians, and you said that this was discussed at the Commission with Colonel Mijatovic, General Loncar, and Kotur. Now, in relation to these armed civilians, the ones you discussed with General Loncar, and General Kotur, and the ones who you say you also saw in the field, are you able to help us with whether these were Albanian armed civilians or Serb armed civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although it was impossible to tell, you know, from that statement who they were, as it was an area where there were Serbs. It was a Serbian area. It's more than likely that they would have been Serbs as opposed to Albanians. Albanian civilians were not normally armed. The only people in the KLA -- sorry, on the Albanian side would have been the KLA; and although they had no uniform, they usually had some vestige of uniform whether it was a white band wrapped around their arm indicating which sort of group they belonged to or so on. So if you saw somebody without any of this, then it was probably a civilian. And in this case it was more likely -- the probability was more likely to be a Serb than it was to be an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to clarify, if you recall, where was it you saw such civilians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually in the Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if you recall, are you able to name any such villages?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many. Top of my head I can't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in terms of time-frame, again if you recall, when did you see these civilians in Serb villages, as you say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would have been in the final part of our, sort of, stay in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Would you be able to clarify the time-frame for that, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly in the last three, four weeks, there about, four or five weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to provide any information on how these Serb civilians obtained their arms, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told by the members of the Commission that they were issued the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And who issued them with these weapons, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- I don't know -- I can't remember exactly, it was the VJ or the MUP; but they were issued locally in the local villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I'd now like to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could call up P836, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you will see on your screen shortly that this is the Shaun Byrnes Agreement. And I would like to take you to paragraph 2 of this document. This is in relation to the process of notification. That's what paragraph 2 is referring to. Now, in relation to paragraph 2 and the notification requirements set out in this paragraph, could you tell us, please, what was your understanding of how this process of notification would operate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there would be some official document, probably following a meeting with the Commission or directly between the MUP and our representative who would first of all inform us and then give us a written document explaining why and what they were intending to do and where, which never happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in terms of time-frame, are you able to provide any information on such meetings, if such notification was ever provided?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, no such information was ever provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up P837, and that's the Clark-Naumann Agreement. And if we could go to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you were shown this paragraph by Defence counsel today. I'm interested in the sentence that refers to the right to respond adequately and proportionately to any form of terrorist activity. When you were asked about this paragraph, you responded saying that the only thing that doesn't apply is the word "proportionality," what do you mean by your statement when you said "proportionality did not apply"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if gunmen are sitting in the house, the sniper are sitting in the house and shooting at the Serbian security forces and causing injury and death, then obviously the legal authorities have the right to deal with him. And you can deal with him in any number of ways, including totally destroying the building in which he is sitting. That's quite fair. It's extreme, but it's fair. But it's unfair to shell the entire village, you know, in order to try and flush him out of the village. And this we know -- we saw a number of times where this sort of thing was happening, including the, sort of, the, again, west of Podujevo and Lapastica, and those sort of areas there where extreme force was used by the MUP against a doctor's house which was, you know, totally destroyed, ransacked and everybody in the area was killed, wiped out. That that was disproportionate, and we did preach proportionality. And that's why when Defence counsel spoke about the area to the south near the salient coming into Kosovo. The reason that the action there carried out by the Serbian security forces was proportionate is, I think, they were beginning to sort of listen to what we were saying because it was, A, giving them bad press. I mean, the terrible thing about disproportionality is the press lives on this, and we were try to say, Look, if you want a better image, if you want to, sort of, be seen as defending yourself against terrorists, then, you know, behave proportionately and appropriately. And I believe that there was a phase when that was happening. And Racak was an example, after Racak, the funeral, as was Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you sir. And in terms of conveying such information on proportionality to the commission, could you comment on how such information was provided, if at all, to the commission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In endless discussions on how we sort of dealt with these types of problems, for example, from our experience working in Northern Ireland which is a sort of similar situation with terrorists and urban warfare with people with no uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to provide a rough figure on how often such issues arose during the meetings that you had with the commission, discussions about proportionality that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say right from the very beginning. It was started even earlier on when General DZ was leading the meetings, and it went on throughout the entire time we were there. It never stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that there was an improvement from the time Racak occurred. Are you able to give an example of an extreme case where proportionality wasn't adhered to as a contrast? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, the -- I mean, we saw an extraordinary thing one day where the troops were -- this is VJ was carrying out a live-fire exercise but against a village. There were two villages down range of the artillery and tanks, and they were just firing, and we said, you know, Why are you doing this? They said, Well, we are training. I said, Aren't the villagers -- aren't there villagers? They said, Yes, but we told them to leave, but they decided that they were going to take these villagers out and just shell the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In terms of time-frame, do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the new year. That was the new year.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In the new year. And the names of the villages, if you recall, or if not, the general vicinity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Vucitrn area again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Moving on to my final topic, this is the UN resolution that was shown to you today by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up D160, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a number of questions today about this UN resolution. Could you tell us, if you know, what were the background circumstances that led to the adoption of this resolution in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a whole series, a whole period of worsening situation in Kosovo, and various, sort of, cease-fires, various lulls. But it got worse and worse and eventually there were a series of activities by the Serbian security forces which hit the headlines and, you know, they have now, sort of, gone into almost Albanian folklore as to what happened in these areas, the deaths that were caused. And they were just, sort of, NATO got involved and as with activation order for the bombing threatened Mr. Milosevic, and that's how it just developed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And this whole period of the worsening situation in Kosovo, are you able to provide a rough time-frame of what this period encompassed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was several years it went over, two or three years.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And these incidences that hit the headlines that were caused by the Serbian security forces, again, if you recall, when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just gone out of my mind, but I think they were somewhere in the area of Klina and that was the sort of area this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the year before, I think, we came in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, brain is drained.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's fine. It's been a long day. Thanks for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I do not have any further questions for you sir, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. You will be pleased to know, Colonel, that we have finished, that you will be able to get away. We thank you once again for your attendance and for the assistance you've been able to give. We are sorry that you had to be -- continue today over the weekend. The court officer will show you out, but we thank you again for your attendance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much, indeed, for your indulgence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Clearly no point in contemplating a fresh witness at this hour. So we will adjourn until tomorrow, but before doing so, could I mention, Ms. Gopalan, or Ms. Kravetz, a concern the Chamber has that the witness notifications for the next two weeks following this week are each for only four witnesses, and they are in each apparent case witnesses with which the Prosecution will not be long. In most cases half an hour, at the most I think an hour. It ought to be possible with, other than extensive witnesses, to finish at least five witnesses in a week, and if we are to keep this Prosecution proceeding at a reasonable pace, we need to set that sort of general objective. There will be longer witnesses unquestionably, and time, as usual, will be allowed. There will be times when witnesses may even be shorter, and we can think of six or seven in a week. But to be setting for relatively routine witnesses, a programme of only four in a five-day week, is in the Chamber's view not an adequate rate of progress. So that if you could convey that to Mr. Stamp and try and ensure that there is some attention to that. And we would ask all counsel to bear in mind our growing concern that we are not making an adequate rate of progress, and the Chamber will therefore become more insistent about the rate at which we progress through the witnesses. Thank you for that. We now adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday the 3rd day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.54 p.m.,
